title: A Day in the House
subtitle: One family, one Saturday, and the vocabulary of every room they walk through.
description: A B1 reading and listening text following a family through a day at home, teaching the everyday vocabulary of rooms, chores and small repairs, with comprehension exercises.
lexicalSet: the subtitle says it: the vocabulary of every room in the house
passage: The sun came through the blinds and woke Sarah before her alarm, which almost never happens and which she decided to treat as a good sign. She stretched, pushed the covers off, and went downstairs.

Her father John was already in the kitchen. The coffee machine was making the noise it makes — a gurgle and then a long hiss — and the smell had reached the stairs before she did. He had the radio on low and was laying the table: plates, bowls, and a handful of silverware he was distributing without much attention to which side anything went on.
Upstairs, her brother Ben was still asleep. His laundry basket had been full for several days and had now reached the stage where clothes were arranged around it rather than in it.

Sarah and John ate scrambled eggs and toast and went through the day. There was a leaky faucet in the upstairs bathroom that had been dripping since Tuesday, and a light bulb in the hallway that had gone and that nobody had replaced because the ceiling there is high and the ladder is in the garage.
Ben came down at half past ten, made a face at the smell of coffee, ate three pieces of toast standing up, and moved to the couch with the remote before anybody could give him a job.

Sarah started a load of washing, which filled the laundry room with the smell of detergent, and then went to deal with the faucet. She got the toolbox from the garage, turned the water off under the sink, took the faucet apart on a towel so the small parts would not roll away, tightened the screw that had worked loose and replaced the rubber washer, which had gone hard and flat. Then she put it back together and turned the water on and nothing leaked, which she enjoyed more than she expected to.
John spent the afternoon in the home office, which is the tidiest room in the house and the only one with a rule about it. Books on the shelves, files in order, and a door he closes.
Ben, having exhausted the television, went out to the yard and threw a ball for the dog for forty minutes. The dog did not get bored before he did.

Sarah's mother Jane came home at six and the two of them made dinner together, which is the part of the week they both protect: chopping, talking, one of them stirring a pot while the other says something and has to repeat it over the noise of the extractor fan. They made a stew, and it filled the downstairs with the smell of it for the rest of the evening.

At some point between the washing machine finishing and the stew being ready, Ben carried the ladder in from the garage without being asked and changed the hallway bulb. Nobody saw him do it. Everybody noticed, because the hallway had been dark for a fortnight and suddenly was not, and nobody said anything about it, which in that house counts as a conversation.

exercises.title: Understanding the Text
exercises.instructions: Read for what the family members are like, which the text shows rather than states.

items.prompt: Why had nobody replaced the hallway bulb?
options: There were no spare bulbs in the house
The ceiling is high and the ladder is in the garage
items.explanation: Two small obstacles, neither serious, which together are enough to stop the job for a fortnight.

items.prompt: How does the writer describe Ben's laundry basket?
options: It had been emptied that morning
It had reached the stage where clothes were arranged around it rather than in it
It was hidden under his bed
items.explanation: A description that gives you his character without using an adjective about him.

items.prompt: Why did Ben move to the couch quickly?
options: Before anybody could give him a job
Because he wanted to watch a particular program
To avoid the smell of coffee
items.explanation: Stated directly, and it sets up the ending.

items.prompt: Why did Sarah take the tap apart on a towel?
options: So the small parts would not roll away
Because the towel was already wet
items.explanation: A real detail from doing the job — the kind of thing you only know if you have lost a washer down a drain.

items.prompt: What was actually wrong with the faucet?
options: A screw had worked loose and the rubber washer had gone hard
items.explanation: Two small things, both fixable in an afternoon with a toolbox.

items.prompt: What does the writer say about Sarah finishing the repair?
options: She enjoyed it more than she expected to
She was annoyed it had taken so long
She decided to call a plumber anyway
items.explanation: The satisfaction of a small competent repair, noted without being made into a lesson.

items.prompt: What does the text say about cooking dinner together?
options: It is the part of the week Sarah and Jane both protect
They take turns so neither has to do it twice
They do it only when Ben is out
items.explanation: “Protect” is doing the work — it implies something they would defend against interruption.

items.prompt: Why does the writer say nobody saying anything about the bulb “counts as a conversation”?
options: The family rarely speaks to each other
Because in that family, noticing and not commenting is how something is acknowledged
Because Ben would have denied doing it
items.explanation: Everybody noticed; nobody mentioned it; the silence is the acknowledgement. It also quietly revises what you thought about Ben.

exercises.title: Around the House
exercises.instructions: Complete each sentence. Several of these differ between American and British English.

items.prompt: The ___ in the bathroom has been ___ since Tuesday.
items.explanation: American faucet, British tap. To drip is to fall in single drops; to leak is the more general word.
To lay the table is to put out the plates and cutlery. “Set the table” is equally common in American English.

items.prompt: I put ___ ___ ___ ___ on before I went out.
items.explanation: A load of washing is one batch through the machine. “A load of laundry” is the more American form.

items.prompt: The screw had ___ ___ over the years.
items.explanation: To work loose is to gradually become less tight through use — the verb does the work of “slowly and by itself”.

items.prompt: The bulb in the hall has ___, and the ___ is in the garage.
items.explanation: A bulb “goes” when it stops working — a very common informal use.

items.prompt: He played with the dog in the ___ for most of the afternoon.
items.explanation: American yard, British garden — for the outdoor space behind a house.

exercises.title: True or False?
exercises.instructions: Decide whether each statement matches the text.

items.statement: Sarah woke up before her alarm.
Sarah called somebody to fix the faucet.
items.explanation: False — she fixed it herself with the toolbox from the garage.

items.statement: The home office is the tidiest room in the house.
items.explanation: True — “and the only one with a rule about it”.

items.statement: The dog got tired before Ben did.
items.explanation: False — “the dog did not get bored before he did”.

items.statement: Ben was asked to change the light bulb.
items.explanation: False — he did it “without being asked”, and nobody saw him.

discussion: Describe your own home room by room, using at least eight words from this text.
Sarah enjoyed fixing the faucet more than she expected. Is there a small repair you have taught yourself?
The bulb went unchanged for a fortnight because of two small obstacles. What is the equivalent in your house?
The family acknowledges Ben's help by not mentioning it. Does your family do things that way, or the opposite?
Write about 150 words describing a Saturday at home, showing what the people are like through what they do rather than by describing them.
